articles.title: FDA approves new treatment for head and neck cancer
articles.description: The FDA approved the use of a new drug, amivantamab, to treat head and neck cancer. The clinical trials were led by Yale School of Medicine researchers.
paragraphs: On Nov. 5, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the use of a new drug to treat head and neck cancer, the first in seven years. Called amivantamab, the drug is the first to target two growth receptors for head and neck cancer simultaneously, reducing the cancer’s ability to adapt to the treatment. The FDA granted amivantamab accelerated approval because of the promising results it showed during clinical trials, which were led by Yale School of Medicine researchers.

Barbara Burtness, MD, Anthony N. Brady Professor of Medicine at Yale School of Medicine, was the lead clinical investigator for the trials. She also guided the Yale portion of the multinational study.
We spoke with Burtness, who serves as co-leader of Yale Cancer Center's Developmental Therapeutics Research Program, about the amivantamab approval and the future of dual-targeted cancer drugs.

Barbara Burtness, MD: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is the sixth most common cancer, and that probably equates to just under 70,000 cases a year. It comes in two main etiologic groups. Some diagnoses are related to human papilloma virus (HPV), and many are not. And the ones that are not are related to environmental exposures like tobacco and alcohol, or sometimes dental complications. This drug, amivantamab, is approved for the second group.

Burtness: For a long time, targeting epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR) was the only targeted therapy available for head and neck cancer. EGFR is a large molecule on the cancer cells. It’s anchored into the cell membrane and it receives growth signals, which it communicates into the cell. This causes the release of chemical signals that then lead the cell to divide and be more resistant to treatment. This receptor is very abundantly expressed on head and neck cancers, particularly the HPV-negative type.

There is a monoclonal antibody called cetuximab that targets just that receptor, and the first ever dose of cetuximab was given here at Yale in 1995. Since then, there has been an enormous amount of research to find a better therapy. When cetuximab was initially developed, it had a response rate of about 12%. More recently, when it's given after immunotherapy, we see a response rate of 24%. But that's still pretty disappointing, and so there's been a lot of research into how the cell is circumventing this lack of EGFR signaling.

Burtness: Amivantamab targets both EGFR and another site simultaneously. Researchers have identified what we call adaptive resistance, meaning as one part of epithelial signaling gets turned down, the cell compensates by increasing the activity of other pathways. One of the most important of these is through another receptor, but in a different family, and this is called mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET).

There's a lot of interest in how you can prevent the cell from compensating for EGFR inhibition by upregulating MET, and one strategy is to give an antibody that targets the ligand for MET, a protein called HGF. The better strategy has been to develop an antibody that binds to EGFR and binds to MET at the same time. Our hypothesis had been that would mean the cells couldn't compensate in the same way. Amivantamab is a treatment that had already been approved in lung cancer, and Yale researchers wanted to test it in head and neck cancer.
articles.lede: The FDA approved the use of a new drug, amivantamab, to treat head and neck cancer. The clinical trials were led by Yale School of Medicine researchers.

articles.title: Whole genome screening identifies opportunities for more patients to benefit from existing therapies
articles.description: Experts argue that we are overlooking substantial opportunities every year to match cancer patients with targeted treatments because current genomic testing and targeted treatment approvals are often organised around where in the body a cancer originates, rather than the tumour’s DNA.
paragraphs: We have approved drugs that we know can target particularly genetic mutations, but if these mutations occur in the wrong type of cancer, we can’t use them

Researchers at the University of Cambridge found one in five primary cancers and one in four metastatic cancers contained changes to their DNA associated with targeted therapies already approved for use in at least one cancer type – but many of these changes occur in cancers where the corresponding treatments are not currently approved or are not routinely tested for.

Targeted therapies have revolutionised treatment for cancers. Identifying the genetic alternations that drive tumours allows doctors to administer highly specific drugs that target those defects. These drugs are approved following extensive clinical trials, typically focused on specific tumour types, with approvals then given for only these cancers.

This means that a drug targeting a molecular pathway commonly seen in ovarian cancer, for example, might be approved for use in this type of cancer. But if the same pathway is also found in pancreatic cancer, the drug cannot be redeployed without further clinical trials. When it comes to rare cancers, these clinical trials can take many years to accrue the numbers of patients required for approvals.

A team led by researchers at the Early Cancer Institute, University of Cambridge, analysed whole-genome sequencing data from more than 17,000 tumours – 11,000 primary cancers from the UK-based 100,000 Genomes Project and 6,000 metastatic cancers from the Netherlands-based Hartwig Medical Foundation – to ask how often potentially targetable genetic changes occur across different cancer types.

The team screened every genome looking for immediately actionable alterations – that is, biomarkers linked to therapies already approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) – as well as for genetic changes linked to drugs currently in development or in clinical trials, but not yet fully approved.

They found that around one in five primary cancers (19%) and one in four metastatic cancers (26%) contained changes to their DNA that could be targeted with existing approved targeted therapies. However, more than half of the potentially actionable DNA changes identified occurred in cancer types other than those for which drug treatments have been granted FDA approval.

Professor Serena Nik-Zainal from the Department of Genomic Medicine at the University of Cambridge, the study’s senior author, said: “The scale of potentially missed opportunities is striking. We have approved drugs that we know can target particularly genetic mutations, but if these mutations occur in the wrong type of cancer, we can’t use them.

“Not every drug will be appropriate for treating a different type of cancer, so not every patient could immediately benefit from existing therapies, but our study identifies opportunities for new clinical trials that could lead to much better outcomes.”

Many languages, one common neural code
articles.description: Analyzing speakers of 21 languages, an MIT study using multilingual AI finds the human brain may represent meaning in much the same way.
paragraphs: Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.
Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way.

Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages.

“Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper.

The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.
Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere.

“Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center.
While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way.
For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker?

It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence.
articles.lede: Analyzing speakers of 21 languages, an MIT study using multilingual AI finds the human brain may represent meaning in much the same way.

articles.title: J-PAL North America launches Medicaid Learning Lab to help state agencies test, learn, and improve health care delivery
cats: Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL)
articles.description: J-PAL North America's new Medicaid Learning Lab will help four state Medicaid agencies in building capacity to use evidence in their decision-making. The program will support the Delaware Department of Health and Social Services, the Louisiana Department of Health, MassHealth, and TennCare.
paragraphs: This fall, J-PAL North America, a regional office of MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, has launched the Medicaid Learning Lab (MLL) in collaboration with the SCALE Lab at the Yale School of Public Health. Through April 2027, this fully funded program will support an inaugural cohort of four state Medicaid agencies: the Delaware Department of Health and Social Services; the Louisiana Department of Health; MassHealth; and TennCare.

A kickoff convening in September brought together more than 20 Medicaid leaders, researchers, and collaborators and was the first opportunity for participants to meet in person before the program's online sessions began. Speakers included researchers from the J-PAL network: Amy Finkelstein, co-scientific director of J-PAL North America and the John and Jennie S. MacDonald Professor of Economics at MIT; Jacob Wallace of Yale University, scientific advisor to the MLL and faculty co-director of the SCALE Lab; and Rebecca Myerson, associate professor at Emory University.

Practitioners also spoke, including Bill Halsey, director of healthcare policy and innovation at the Connecticut Department of Social Services; Allison Espeseth of Covering Wisconsin; and Hannah Maniates, director of Medicaid programming at the National Association of Medicaid Directors.

Halsey described why testing and learning in Medicaid matters: “Often in Medicaid, we will implement a new program and only years later will we evaluate it. If we have a test-and-learn mentality, where we set up a rigorous evaluation methodology before implementing a new program, we can establish a rapid-learning cycle and generate actionable insights in a shorter time frame."
Maniates named the questions agencies most often bring to researchers: What makes member outreach effective? What works for automatic renewals? And how do changes in enrollment affect utilization?

The MLL is the latest iteration of J-PAL North America's Learning Lab model, following the Climate Action Learning Lab, which has now run twice with state and local climate leaders, and the AprendeLab in Puerto Rico. The MLL also builds on J-PAL North America's prior work to launch randomized evaluations with Medicaid agencies in South Carolina, Wisconsin, Connecticut, and Maine.

Connecticut's evaluation efforts demonstrate where MLL participants' engagement can lead: a single J-PAL-supported evaluation of adolescent vaccination outreach grew into a sustained partnership between the state's Department of Social Services and Yale researchers, with data scientists now embedded in the agency.

Closing the convening, Wallace told the cohort that Connecticut may look like the exception, but it is not. Their evaluation was initiated from the same place that MLL participants currently stand, working to identify one program and one question worth answering.

The MLL is launching at a time when Medicaid leaders are under growing pressure to improve health outcomes while controlling costs. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) together cover more than 74 million people and account for roughly 30 percent of average total state spending, and new cuts and implementation requirements mean state leaders are being asked to do more with less. The program will support participating agencies in using evidence to determine what works, make informed trade-offs, and direct dollars toward programs with proven impact.
articles.lede: J-PAL North America's new Medicaid Learning Lab will help four state Medicaid agencies in building capacity to use evidence in their decision-making.

Watson Lecture: Sarkis Mazmanian Explores the Connection Between the Gut Microbiome and the Brain
articles.description: What if understanding the brain—and treating some neurological diseases—began in the gut? On Wednesday, December 2nd, 2026, Sarkis Mazmanian, the Luis B. & Nelly Soux Professor of Microbiology and a Merkin Institute Professor, will discuss how his laboratory investigates the complex relationship between the trillions of microbes living in our digestive system and the health and function of the brain.
paragraphs: That question is at the center of research by Caltech microbiologist Sarkis Mazmanian, the Luis B. & Nelly Soux Professor of Microbiology and a Merkin Institute Professor, whose laboratory investigates the complex relationship between the trillions of microbes living in our digestive system and the health and function of the brain.

One major focus of Mazmanian's research is Parkinson's disease. His group has found evidence that gut microbes and the molecules they produce can contribute to inflammation and movement-related symptoms, opening new avenues for understanding how the disease develops. Some discoveries from his laboratory have already helped form the basis of ongoing clinical trials in humans.

"The vast majority of individuals who are diagnosed with Parkinson's have gastrointestinal symptoms," Mazmanian said. "We thought to ourselves, maybe that's a clue that the gut microbiome was involved in Parkinson's. And so, we set out several years ago to essentially test our hypothesis."

Mazmanian was born in Beirut, Lebanon, and moved to Los Angeles with his family when he was three years old. Although he showed an early curiosity about how things worked, often taking apart household objects to understand them, he didn't discover his passion for science until college. He initially enrolled as an English major, drawn to literature and writing, but a general biology elective sparked his interest in the natural world and scientific discovery. As he explored different fields, he became particularly interested in research and chose to major in microbiology at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), where he developed a lasting fascination with microbes.

On Wednesday, December 2, 2026, at 7:30 p.m. in Beckman Auditorium, Mazmanian's Watson Lecture Trust Your Gut: Microbiome Influences on Brain Health and Disease will explore how gut bacteria communicate with the brain through the nervous and immune systems, as well as molecules produced by microbes. His research is revealing how these interactions can influence behavior, brain function, and neurological disease.
Join us to discover how microscopic organisms living within us could hold important clues to understanding the brain—and perhaps change the future of neurological medicines.
Starting at the Watson Lecture preshow at 6 p.m., members of Mazmanian's lab will be present to answer questions about their research.

The Watson Lectures offer new opportunities each month to hear how Caltech researchers are tackling society's most pressing challenges and inventing the technologies of the future. Join a community of curiosity outside Beckman Auditorium to enjoy food, drinks, and music together before each lecture. Interactive displays related to the evening's topic will give audience members additional context and information. The festivities start at 6 p.m. Guests are also encouraged to stay for post-talk coffee and tea as well as the chance to chat with attendees and researchers.

Advance registration for Mazmanian's talk is full. Guests who have not registered are still welcome to attend the preshow, which does not require registration, beginning at 6 p.m., featuring food, music, and interactive displays.

articles.title: How sensory neurons help the brain pursue its goals
articles.description: A new Yale study reveals how sensory neurons of living animals adjust their responses to environmental changes based on learned preferences, offering new insight into how experience shapes behavior.
paragraphs: A new Yale study offers insight into a fundamental question in neuroscience: How does the nervous system transform sensory information into signals that help us achieve our goals?

It turns out that sensory neurons — specialized nerve cells that transmit environmental information gleaned through the five senses to the brain — may play a more complex role than previously believed.

For the study, the research team trained roundworms to prefer certain temperature conditions using food rewards. They constructed a gradient in which there were different temperatures in given spots; after placing the worms on the gradient, researchers found that the animals inched toward the temperature they’d learned to prefer.

“They remember the temperature at which they were under favorable conditions happily eating, and they go back to that temperature,” said study’s lead author Daniel Colón-Ramos, the Dorys McConnell Duberg Professor of Neuroscience and Cell Biology at Yale School of Medicine.

But deep inside the worm’s nervous system, something unexpected was taking place. Temperature- sensing neurons are known to respond to temperature changes, but not all temperature changes are represented the same way by the worm’s sensory neurons. The sensory neurons sensed changes in temperature throughout the gradient, the researchers found, but turned up their responses when the worm was near the temperature it had learned to prefer and switched the response down when the worm was off course.

The findings may offer a broader lesson about the brain and how it achieves goals. Sensory neurons throughout the animal kingdom detect changes in light, sound, chemicals, and other environmental features. But how an animal navigates depends not only on the stimulus itself, but also on the animal’s prior experience and what it is trying to accomplish.

“Our study shows how a sensory neuron combines information about changes in the environment with information from a learned goal,” said co-first author Malcom Díaz García, a Ph.D. student at Vanderbilt University who was previously part of Colón-Ramos’ Yale lab. “It starts in the way the sensory cell itself represents the experience. The sensory cell is capable of sophisticated computation to represent the environment differently based on a learned goal. This offers a framework for understanding how experience can shape what the nervous system emphasizes and transforms into behavior.”
The study may also help in the understanding of conditions that affect focus and sensory information — such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

“From a molecular perspective, many of our sensory cells are, number one, sensing changes, and number two, using very similar mechanisms to the ones that the sensory cells in the worm are using,” said Sandeep Kumar, a postdoctoral associate at Yale School of Medicine and co-first author of the study. “We have maybe been underestimating how sensory systems are actually plastically representing things based on goals.”
articles.lede: A new Yale study reveals how sensory neurons of living animals adjust their responses to environmental changes based on learned preferences, offering new insight into how experience shapes behavior.

articles.title: Cambridge co-leading world’s largest trial to use AI to help detect breast cancers earlier
articles.description: Women are being invited to take part in a landmark national trial using artificial intelligence to support specialist clinicians and help detect breast cancers earlier. Nearly 700,000 women will take part in the trial.
paragraphs: EDITH will test whether an AI-assisted mammogram-reading tool can help experts review images more efficiently, while maintaining professional oversight and the standards women expect from NHS breast screening

The £10 million NIHR-funded trial is the largest in the world to use an artificial intelligence-assisted tool in breast cancer screening. Cambridgeshire is the first location to launch the trial, which will soon be running at 30 breast screening sites across the UK.
All women aged 50-71 are invited for screening every three years. Currently around 2.1 million women in the UK have breast screening each year, which helps prevent around 1,300 deaths.

Reviewing breast screening x-rays (mammograms) is time intensive. Currently, each mammogram is reviewed by two specialist radiologists. Fewer than 1% of mammograms show signs of cancer, so significant time is spent reviewing negative screening images.

In the trial, known as EDITH, the AI-assisted tool will be used alongside specialists checking the images to look for cancers that are too small to see or feel. This could mean many mammograms would only need to be reviewed by one radiologist and would free-up radiologists to spend more time on diagnosis and caring for women with cancer.

The NHS offers mammograms at local breast screening clinics in GP practices or hospitals, or women can attend one of their local mobile screening vans, conveniently located in supermarket or community car parks.

The trial will not change what happens during a woman’s breast screening appointment. It only affects how the collected images may be reviewed. Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one human radiologist.

To mark the opening of the trial, the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, Yvette Cooper MP, visited the Breast Unit at Addenbrooke’s Hospital to meet with the leaders of the trial, Professor Fiona Gilbert from the University of Cambridge and Addenbrooke’s Hospital and Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips at the University of Warwick.

Speaking on her visit, Yvette Cooper, said: “This is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world, backed by £10 million of government investment to speed up diagnosis and potentially deliver life-saving improvements.

Ultrasound imaging without the gel
articles.description: A stretchy new material could eliminate the need for gel in ultrasound imaging. The rubbery material, developed at MIT and SMART, enabled a wearable ultrasound device to generate clear images over nine days, even during vigorous exercise.

Engineers at MIT and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology’s Wearable Imaging for Tranforming Elderly Care project (SMART WITEC) have developed a dry and stretchy material that could eliminate the need for a wet and sticky gel in ultrasound imaging.

Ultrasound technicians typically spread a cold gel onto a patient’s skin before imaging the area with an ultrasound probe. The gel fills in tiny gaps between the probe and the skin so ultrasound waves can travel efficiently through the skin to generate clear images of a patient’s underlying structures.

Members of MIT’s Zhao Lab are designing wearable ultrasound patches that could provide continuous imaging, at home or on the go. But one sticking point has been the gel. Their previous designs have included a layer of hydrogel — a mostly water-based material that seals up the space between the skin and a small ultrasound probe. But within a day or two, the gel can dry out, along with its ability to transmit sound waves.

“In a doctor’s office, a technician can simply apply more gel if needed. But for a wearable device, gel-based designs can limit their long-term usability,” says Xuanhe Zhao, the Uncas and Helen Whitaker Professor of Mechanical Engineering at MIT.

The MIT team has developed a liquid-free alternative to gel that efficiently transmits ultrasound waves, which they report today in the journal Science. Because the material is dry from the start, its performance remains stable over long periods. In experiments, the engineers found that the rubbery material enabled a wearable ultrasound device to generate clear, continuous images over nine days, even during vigorous exercise.

As a demonstration, the team fixed a small wearable patch, about the size of a key fob, to a volunteer’s neck. The patch contained a small ultrasound probe, and the dry and stretchy layer that stuck directly to the skin. The entire patch was connected to a small portable tablet that recorded the patch’s ultrasound images as the volunteer took a 30-minute bike ride, from MIT’s campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, to Bunker Hill in neighboring Charlestown, and back.
“We are really aiming to address a material challenge in ultrasound imaging,” says study leader Shu Wang, a postdoc in MIT’s Department of Mechanical Engineering.

“If you don’t have a good interface, that will definitely stop you from developing this wearable imaging field,” adds co-lead author and MIT postdoc Runze Li. “This is a very good solution that enables a longer time for imaging.”

In addition to Zhao, Wang, and Li, the study’s MIT co-authors are Chen Gong and Won Jun Song; additional co-authors are Zihan Tang and Ying Li of the University of Wisconsin at Madison; Chwee Teck Lim of the National University of Singapore; and Xiaodong Chen of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Zhao, Chen, and Lim are the co-lead principal investigators of the SMART WITEC interdisciplinary research group.

Confirmed: Numbers tell, but language sells
articles.description: When people want to persuade their audience that a statistic is high or low, relatively more of them use language to describe the data, rather than stating the original numbers, a new study shows.
paragraphs: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."

Suppose you are in charge of your firm’s commuting policy and, after some research, you determine that 57 percent of your colleagues drive to work. How would you communicate that number to co-workers?

You could just tell them the number. Or you could characterize it in words. If you want to imply that 57 percent is a large number, you could call it “a clear majority,” or even “approaching two-thirds” (roughly 67 percent). However, if you seek to minimize 57 percent, you might call it “barely over half.”

Either way, when people are motivated to persuade their audience that a number is particularly high or low, they are considerably more likely to use language to describe the data, rather than simply airing the original numbers.

Now a new study co-authored by an MIT scholar quantifies this phenomenon: People motivated to persude others about statistical facts are 25 percent to 29 percent more likely to use words describing the numbers in question, instead of the numbers themselves. That is a large enough increase to be termed “substantial,” “significant,” or any number of other words.

“If I’m a well-informed expert and I have incentives to persuade my audience, I’m relatively more likely to choose to use language,” says co-author Victor de Chaisemartin, a doctoral candidate at the MIT Sloan School of Management.

The language that experts choose when seeking to persuade others is also more slanted than their numeric communications. As the authors note in the paper, people appear to be leveraging the imprecision of language in ways they feel are palatable: Whereas reporting a number incorrectly would be precisely false, it may be more psychologically comfortable to slant a message using language.
And that’s just the half of it. The study also shows that audiences find language-based descriptions of numbers convincing — even when they are told there is an agenda behind them.

“Language messages are particularly persuasive,” de Chaisemartin says. Telling an audience they are being spun, he notes, “actually doesn’t do very much to mitigate this. That’s interesting. It makes you wonder what’s going through people’s heads, and how they are dealing with information.”

The paper, “ Numbers Tell, Words Sell ,” is being published in the American Economic Review. The authors are de Chaisemartin; Michael Thaler, a lecturer in economics at University College London; and Mattie Toma, an associate professor at the University of Warwick.
articles.lede: When people want to persuade their audience that a statistic is high or low, relatively more of them use language to describe the data, rather than stating the original numbers, a new study shows.

articles.title: Can This Blood Test Reveal a Grim Brain Disease in Living Patients?
articles.description: A new study shows for the first time that a blood test could help identify advanced stages of a devastating brain disease found to be rampant among former professional football players. Currently, the condition, chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), can only be diagnosed after death.
paragraphs: The study is led by Boston University with participation from researchers at 20 institutions, including Gil Rabinovici, MD, from the Edward and Pearl Fein Memory and Aging Center at UC San Francisco. He serves as co-principal investigator and PET imaging lead.
The study was published in JAMA on Nov. 19 and funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

CTE is characterized by mood and behavioral changes in its early stages and later by cognitive impairment and motor symptoms. As many as 3 in 4 deceased NFL players had CTE, a study published last month found. The disease also occurs in former players of other contact sports, victims of repeated blows to the head, and military veterans exposed to blast waves from explosives.

In the study, researchers analyzed blood samples taken before death from 21 former American football players who participated in previous studies. Autopsies later showed that 18 of the 21 had CTE: 16 had high-stage disease and two had low-stage disease.

Blood levels of eMTBR-tau were significantly higher among participants with high-stage CTE than those with low-stage or no CTE. The study did not show a clear difference between low-stage CTE and no CTE, and it was too small to establish the test’s diagnostic accuracy in individual patients.

While these findings are “very preliminary,” if validated in follow-up studies, the blood test could be used “to support a diagnosis of CTE in people who have had repetitive head impacts and are experiencing neurological symptoms,” said Rabinovici, who holds the Edward and Pearl Fein Distinguished Professorship in Memory and Aging.

“In the right clinical context, a positive blood test could be used as an inclusion criterion for testing new drugs, which is especially exciting in light of the major advances in tau-targeting therapies,” Rabinovici added, referring to drugs in development to treat Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias.

“Ultimately, our hope is that earlier and more precise detection will help us match patients with the right treatments at the right time and improve outcomes,” said corresponding author Michael Alosco, PhD, from Boston University CTE Center and Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center.

Four of the participants with CTE also had Alzheimer’s disease-related brain changes, and eMTBR-tau levels were highest in this group. The researchers also measured p-tau217, a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer’s disease, to help distinguish between the two diseases. Higher blood levels of eMTBR-tau were associated with a greater burden of abnormal tau in brain regions affected by CTE at autopsy, while p-tau217 was not.
articles.lede: A new study shows for the first time that a blood test could help identify advanced stages of a devastating brain disease found to be rampant among former professional football players.

Video games may reduce rise in pre-surgery anxiety in children
articles.description: A study by Yale’s Department of Anesthesiology found that playing a driving-themed video game immediately before surgery may reduce the rise in pre-surgery
paragraphs: A racing video game may seem out of place in the operating room, but it could help with pre-surgery anxiety. A study by Yale’s Department of Anesthesiology published in the Journal of Clinical Anesthesia found that playing a driving-themed video game immediately before surgery may reduce the rise in pre-surgery anxiety in children ages 4 to 14. The children were undergoing procedures with general anesthesia.

Pre-surgery anxiety in children is common and can complicate care. It has been associated with a difficult recovery, highlighting the importance of anxiety management to help reduce stress in young patients before surgery.

Anthony Longhini, MD, assistant professor of anesthesiology and principal investigator on the study, cares for pediatric patients at Yale New Haven Hospital. Working with his team, he used a portable Bedside Entertainment and Relaxation Theater (BERT) system. The BERT setup enhanced the video game-based intervention.

“It was a Lego Batman racing game, because it’s the kind of thing that stays on the track, even if you’re not using the steering wheel, so the child can be either passively or actively steering,” says Longhini. “It’s not violent or complex. It’s something that a small three-year-old or an older child can use.”

When describing his work, Longhini emphasized the team’s interest in using video game technology that would allow the patient to still be aware of the room around them. The BERT allowed patients to be actively engaged while still being aware of the surrounding operating room staff.
"We thought that, by adding an active element to it, the child would be engaged further than they would by just watching a screen or holding a tablet."

“We wanted to avoid using a passive device that would be more similar to a large TV or an iPad,” says Longhini. “It has some novelty because it’s large and it’s not something they see all the time. We thought that, by adding an active element to it, the child would be engaged further than they would by just watching a screen or holding a tablet.”
The operating room staff responded well to the device, even though it was new to their busy workspace.

“We surveyed the operating room staff, and a lot of them were excited to see it come out,” says Longhini. “The projector has a clamp that would go onto the operating table, and then the screen would sit at the bottom of the bed. The staff began to help set it up and take it down for each patient, which was nice. I was surprised by how accepted it was.”

The team found that the patients in the BERT group had significantly smaller increases in anxiety before induction of anesthesia than those who received standard care. The immersive video game experience engaged surgical patients and distracted them from worrying about their procedures.
articles.lede: A racing video game may seem out of place in the operating room, but it could help with pre-surgery anxiety.

articles.title: Engineered Nanosyringes Open a New Route into Plant Cells
articles.description: Caltech researchers reprogrammed bacterial injection machines to recognize plant cells and deliver active proteins, introducing new possibilities for studying and engineering plants
paragraphs: Understanding and improving plants often requires changing what happens inside their cells. Proteins control how cells grow, respond to stress, and carry out countless other tasks. Delivering these molecular tools directly into plant cells could give researchers new ways to study those processes and engineer useful traits. But getting active proteins past the cell wall and membrane that protect each plant cell remains a major obstacle.

Now a team of Caltech researchers has adapted tiny bacterial "nanosyringes" to recognize plant cells and inject proteins into them. The system delivered enzymes that rearrange DNA and enable targeted gene insertion in leaf cells, establishing a new route for bringing functional molecular tools into plants. The advance could support research across plant biology and biotechnology, with longer-term applications in crop improvement.

"One of the biggest barriers to studying and improving plants is getting useful biomolecules inside their cells," says Gozde Demirer, the Clare Boothe Luce Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering and corresponding author of a paper about the work that appears in the journal Nature Nanotechnology.

"We constantly hear about groundbreaking technologies in human medicine, but this feels like a massive step to bridge the gap between those breakthroughs and the agricultural sector," says Mark G. Legendre, the lead author of the new paper and a chemical engineering graduate student in Demirer's lab. "While our platform still requires more development before it might be deployed in the field, we're confident that we can eventually produce the first plant transformation system with cell-targeting and multifunctional capabilities."

Many existing approaches to genetic modification in plants introduce DNA instructions that tell cells to make a desired protein. Delivering the protein itself bypasses that step, which reduces the chance of unwanted DNA ending up in the plant's genome. With further development, the new approach using modified nanosyringes could also offer more control over when and where a molecular tool acts, whether the goal is a temporary change in cell behavior or a lasting change to the genome.

The Caltech team adapted an injection system originally found in bacteria from the genus Photorhabdus. In nature, these bacteria release tiny syringes that deliver toxins into insect cells. The bacterial tail fibers recognize and attach to a target cell. Then a surrounding sheath contracts, driving an inner tube through the cell membrane. The researchers engineered the system, produced it in laboratory bacteria, and applied the purified particles to plant cells.

To make the tail fibers attach to plant cells instead of insect cells, the scientists replaced their natural binding region with a short chain of amino acids called flg22. Many plants have an immune receptor called FLS2 (FLAGELLIN SENSITIVE 2) on the surface of their cells that recognizes flg22 as a sign of bacterial infection. So displaying flg22 on the nanosyringes gave the tail fibers a molecular attachment point on plant cells.
articles.lede: Understanding and improving plants often requires changing what happens inside their cells. Proteins control how cells grow, respond to stress, and carry out countless other tasks.

UCSF Launches Large-Scale Study of Psychedelics in the Real World
articles.description: UCSF researchers are launching CANOPY, an ambitious effort to study psychedelics in the real world, tracking thousands of people before and after psychedelic experiences to understand their effects on the brain, body and well-being.
paragraphs: Most psychedelic experiences don’t happen in research labs. To better understand their effects, UC San Francisco scientists are going where the experiences are and launching a global study to track what psychedelics do to people’s brains, bodies and well-being.

CANOPY will follow as many as 3,000 people around the world who plan to take psychedelics at home, organized retreats, and other settings, to see how the drugs affect their mood, well-being, and other psychological outcomes. Some of the study participants also will undergo brain imaging and provide physiological and biological data.

“Psychedelics are widely used outside research labs, yet much of what we know about their effects comes from carefully controlled research settings,” Carhart-Harris said. “CANOPY gives us an opportunity to bring scientific rigor to these experiences at a scale we haven’t had before — to understand not just whether psychedelics can be beneficial, but for whom, under what circumstances, and why.”

Unlike a traditional clinical trial, researchers will not provide participants with psychedelics or determine what they take. Instead, they will enroll people who are already planning to use psychedelics for a trial that will be done mostly remotely.

The study will encompass a broad range of psychedelics, including psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca, and ibogaine, as well as MDMA, and ketamine. Participants will complete standardized assessments before and after psychedelic use and for up to six months afterward.

Those who can travel to UCSF will undergo brain imaging and EEG and provide blood and saliva samples before their planned psychedelic experiences; and they will use wearable devices to collect physiological data outside the lab.

Researchers hope CANOPY will help explain why psychedelic experiences can produce dramatically different outcomes from one person to another. They hope to disentangle the effects of the drug from individual, biological, psychological, and environmental factors that are associated with beneficial or adverse outcomes over time.

The project is also designed as a research platform for more targeted studies. Researchers hope the data will both inform future clinical trials and help scientists assess the risks and benefits of using psychedelics outside controlled research settings.

Researchers are recruiting adults who are already planning to use a psychedelic and are willing to complete research assessments. UCSF does not provide psychedelics or direct participants to obtain or use them. The main study is conducted remotely.
articles.lede: UCSF researchers are launching CANOPY, an ambitious effort to study psychedelics in the real world, tracking thousands of people before and after psychedelic experiences to understand their effects on the brain, body…

How to Find Better Treatments Faster for Rare Childhood Brain Tumors
articles.description: UCSF’s Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium advances clinical trials and new treatments for rare childhood brain tumors through global research partnerships.
paragraphs: Brain tumors are the leading cause of cancer-related death among children in the U.S. And many pediatric brain tumors are so rare that no single hospital sees enough patients to answer critical questions or test promising treatments quickly.

UC San Francisco pediatric neuro-oncologists Sabine Mueller, MD, PhD, and Michael Prados, MD, wanted to change that. In 2012, after decades of limited progress against some of the most difficult-to-treat childhood brain tumors, they founded PNOC to bring researchers and institutions together to help accelerate the search for better treatments.

What began with six institutions has grown into a network of nearly 300 pediatric brain tumor specialists at 43 centers around the world. Together, PNOC researchers have conducted 40 clinical trials involving more than 1,400 pediatric patients.

Today, PNOC is leading international clinical trials — including work funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) — to find new ways to learn from patient data across institutions and develop new treatment approaches.

The associated PNOC Foundation, formed to support PNOC, helps fund the consortium’s research and clinical trials. Allyn and Bruce Campbell, whose son was successfully treated for a brain tumor at UCSF, established the foundation in 2013. The goal was to help create a model that could more quickly move discoveries from the lab to children, regardless of where they lived.

“We want every child with brain cancer to have access to the best treatments possible and not only survive but thrive,” said Allyn and Bruce Campbell. “With additional funding from foundations, industry, and governments, we can turn more research into real treatments for more children around the country and world.”

Fewer than 5,000 children are diagnosed with a brain tumor in the U.S. each year. For the rarest types, the patient population is small and widely dispersed across the country, making it difficult to enroll enough children in traditional clinical trials.

PNOC’s model brings together physicians, researchers, patients, and families across institutions and countries to study rare brain tumors that no single center can explore alone. PNOC is helping lead international trials that allow researchers to test several treatments using the same basic trial structure.

One of those studies focuses on diffuse midline glioma (DMG), a rare and aggressive pediatric brain tumor that develops in midline structures of the central nervous system, most commonly the brainstem. Fewer than 10% of brainstem located DMG of children survive two years after diagnosis.

In 2025, research from PNOC’s DMG working group, led by UCSF in collaboration with partners including the University of Michigan, contributed to the FDA’s accelerated approval of the first-of-its-kind treatment for DMG with a specific genetic mutation.
articles.lede: UCSF’s Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium advances clinical trials and new treatments for rare childhood brain tumors through global research partnerships.

A growing public health worry: Prolonged sitting
articles.description: Most Americans are sedentary 6-8 hours a day, elevating their risk for heart disease and cancer, say experts
paragraphs: Most American adults spend six to eight hours per day sitting. Health experts have taken note. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has recommended that people “move more and sit less” to help lower the risk of chronic diseases associated with sedentary behavior.

Over the past decade, a growing body of research has focused on the role of sedentary behavior — including sitting, reclining, or lying down — on poor health outcomes. Study after study points to the importance of avoiding prolonged sitting — more than eight hours a day — to reduce its adverse health effects.
The growing interest corresponds with changes in the workplace as computers have increasingly taken over tasks that used to get workers on their feet in the past, such as copying and scanning.

“Now, you can sit at your desk, and you don’t really have to move,” said I-Min Lee, a leading expert in physical activity and health whose research has helped shape public health guidelines. “We just don’t move around as much these days.”

Studies have shown that prolonged sitting is associated with worse cardiometabolic health, which over time can lead to a higher risk of diabetes, heart disease, and early death, said Lee. Sitting too much can reduce blood flow, weaken blood vessel function, and impair glucose and insulin processing, she added.

“Those who are more sedentary are at higher risk,” said Lee, a Harvard Medical School professor of medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and a professor of epidemiology in the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. “Your risk climbs with more sitting. Once you get above seven to nine hours of sitting a day, the risk really goes up more steeply. The more you sit, the worse off you are.”

Even regular physical activity cannot completely counteract all the harmful effects of too much sitting, research has shown. A 2025 study, published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, examined the association between daily time spent sitting and future risk of four common cardiovascular diseases — atrial fibrillation, heart attack, heart failure, and death from cardiovascular causes — and whether the risk might be offset by physical activity.

The study found that individuals who sat more were more likely to develop those four cardiovascular diseases, said Ezimamaka Ajufo, an HMS clinical fellow in medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and the study’s lead author. It also found that while physical activity can completely neutralize the risk of atrial fibrillation and heart attack, it can only partly offset the risk of heart failure and cardiovascular death.

“We found that sitting was associated with substantially higher risk of cardiovascular disease, heart failure, and cardiovascular death, in particular, when you sat for more than 10.6 hours per day,” said Ajufo. “Avoiding excessive sitting is important for cardiovascular health, especially heart failure and cardiovascular death risk, even if you’re physically active.”

Using statistical modeling, the study also showed that those risks could be substantially reduced by substituting sedentary time for other types of activity. Based on those findings, Ajufo supports taking breaks, or “activity snacks,” to reduce sitting.
articles.lede: Most American adults spend six to eight hours per day sitting. Health experts have taken note.

articles.title: From womb to world: New atlas traces development of key human brain cells
articles.description: UCLA co-led study maps gene regulation in the developing basal ganglia and identifies cells linked to genetic risk for schizophrenia.
paragraphs: A research team co-led by UCLA has created a detailed map of how brain cells develop before and after birth, offering new insight into how the brain grows and how certain neurological and psychiatric conditions may emerge. Published in Cell, the study traces the development of cells in and around the basal ganglia, a group of brain structures that help control movement, habits, reward and behavior and are involved in conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, addiction and schizophrenia.

The research is part of the National Institutes of Health’s BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, a collaborative effort among neuroscientists, computational biologists and software engineers that aims to create a comprehensive atlas of the human brain to help scientists understand how the brain develops and which cells may be involved in neurological and psychiatric conditions.

“Genetic studies can tell us that particular regions of the genome are associated with disease, but they often can’t tell us which cell type is affected or when during development that genetic risk becomes relevant,” said co-senior author Chongyuan Luo, an associate professor of human genetics at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “This atlas gives us that cellular and developmental context.”

That added layer of information can help researchers connect genetic risk for disease to particular cell types and stages of brain development. Tracking where brain cells come from and how they change as they mature has been a big challenge, as some begin in temporary structures that largely disappear around birth. Researchers addressed this by examining those structures directly, following cells from their starting points to where they eventually settle, providing a much clearer picture of how different brain cells develop over time.

Using a technology co-developed by Luo’s lab, researchers analyzed over 155,000 cell nuclei from nine developing human brains, collecting data on DNA regulation from mid-pregnancy to seven months after birth. This analysis, combined with earlier data, included nearly 287,000 cells. Their research showed how cells in the human basal ganglia develop from midpregnancy through infancy, with different cell populations maturing on different timelines and undergoing major changes in how their DNA is regulated and organized.

By comparing the atlas with genetic studies of psychiatric disorders, researchers also found that spiny projection neurons — a major type of neuron in the basal ganglia — showed especially strong overlap with genetic variants associated with schizophrenia.
articles.lede: UCLA co-led study maps gene regulation in the developing basal ganglia and identifies cells linked to genetic risk for schizophrenia.

Can a scent really sharpen your memory? UCLA research suggests the answer is complicated
articles.description: The findings from the study suggest that novelty might be more important than the scent itself, especially as people age.
paragraphs: The sense of smell shares an intimate but mysterious connection with memory. We know that past experiences can flash vividly to mind if we smell a scent that accompanied them. This has led to claims that aromatherapy can enhance memory or even diminish cognitive decline. But the mechanisms by which the brain associates experience with scent are still being unraveled, and there is mixed scientific evidence to back up such claims.

New research from UCLA suggests the answer is more complicated than you might think. The researchers found that young and older adults who completed memory tasks in rooms with lavender essential oil diffused did not perform significantly better than people in unscented rooms. But there was a catch: Older adults who encountered the scent during the first learning phase performed better than people who encountered it during the second. This suggests that novelty plays a role in binding the scent to experience, especially as we age. Perhaps it’s not the type of scent, but the newness of it that boosts memory.
The finding, published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience, adds to what scientists are learning about the relationship between the sense of smell and Alzheimer’s disease.

“There’s been interesting work linking age-related olfactory dysfunction to Alzheimer’s disease, which has sparked interest in using changes in olfaction as an early detection tool,” said UCLA neuroscientist and corresponding author Stephanie Leal. “We designed our study to think about how olfactory cues might be able to modify memory in the context of olfactory dysfunction.”

Leal and colleagues at Rice University recruited young and older volunteers, all of whom were healthy and had no signs of Alzheimer’s. They used a standard olfaction test to establish baseline olfactory functioning. Half the participants entered a room already scented by a lavender essential oil diffuser. Lavender was chosen because it is a common scent many people are already familiar with and may find pleasant or unpleasant. The other half entered an unscented room. The volunteers then looked at two sets of images of everyday household objects on a computer screen, such as a blow dryer or tomato, that varied in the number of overlapping features they had. Participants who viewed the first block in the odor condition viewed the second block of images in the non-odor condition, and vice versa.

After a delay, the researchers showed participants images that were identical to, slightly different from, or entirely different from the ones they had previously seen. During this recall portion of the experiment, many of the objects were slightly altered. For instance, a blow dryer that was red in the learning phase was blue in the recall phase, and participants had to remember whether they had seen the object before but also whether it was identical to the image they had previously viewed. This was designed to test general recall — the memory of seeing a type of object — as well as detail memory, such as the object’s color. They also asked other questions, such as how pleasant participants found the scent.
articles.lede: The findings from the study suggest that novelty might be more important than the scent itself, especially as people age.

articles.title: Heatwaves are threatening Europe’s power supplies, researchers warn
articles.description: After another punishing European summer, electricity suppliers are being warned that climate change is placing power grids under increasing strain, and at possible risk of collapse.
paragraphs: An international team of researchers have shown how heatwaves impact European countries’ ability to generate and supply power, and how they pose an increasing threat to vital national infrastructure.

The team, from the University of Cambridge, City University of Hong Kong, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen), have developed the first open-source toolkit to help national operators understand the different ways that high heat affects their power grid.

According to the researchers’ model simulations, France, Spain and Italy are at highest risk of supply bottlenecks and possible grid failure. Germany and the UK were comparatively more resilient, although the researchers say that the increasing frequency and severity of heatwaves also place their grids at risk of failure, especially after Earth has just experienced its hottest August on record.

“We hope power providers will use these tools to identify vulnerabilities in their systems and take necessary action to stop them collapsing during future heatwaves,” said co-corresponding author Professor Srinivasan Keshav from Cambridge’s Department of Computer Science and Technology.

The results, reported in the journal Nature Energy, are based on a long-term study of the heatwaves of 2019, 2022 and 2024. The researchers used these in their exploration of the interlinked ways that heatwaves put strain on electricity grids.

Heatwaves increase demand for cooling, leading to spikes in electricity consumption. Meanwhile, total power supply falls because, as heat rises, solar panels lose efficiency, and both conventional and nuclear output are cut to prevent overheating. The same high pressure patterns that bring hot weather often also bring low winds, causing wind farms to falter, which further exacerbates the problem.

Power lines, too, must have their load reduced to stop them hitting their heat limits, and are at higher risk of breaking as they sag in the heat. When taken together, these connected issues can lead to supply bottlenecks and what is called load shedding: intentional power cuts to reduce demand and protect power systems.

While these are known problems, the researchers say that conventional models and analyses to date have revealed only parts of the problem and only at a high computational cost. So, they developed their own algorithms to try and capture the full picture of what is going on with a lower computational burden.

“Once you combine all the factors together — demand increase, generator capacity decrease, transmission capacity decrease — you can discover hidden bottleneck regions that existing methods can't find. I think that's the most surprising outcome of our simulations,” said lead author Professor Enming Liang from City University of Hong Kong.
articles.lede: After another punishing European summer, electricity suppliers are being warned that climate change is placing power grids under increasing strain, and at possible risk of collapse.

Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
cats: Institute for Medical Engineering and Science (IMES)
articles.description: MIT researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help remove debris from the brain during sleep, are significantly reduced in older adults.
paragraphs: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

The researchers found that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help remove debris from the brain, are significantly reduced in older adults. This impairment is linked to a decrease in the slow brain waves that normally occur during deep sleep, the researchers found, and is not just a result of getting less sleep.

The researchers now hope to explore whether the disruption of CSF flow increases the risk of neurodegenerative disorders, and if any of the sleep patterns they observed might offer a way to predict an individual’s risk.

“We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes,” says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT’s Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.
Her lab also plans to investigate whether there might be any interventions that could improve CSF flow in older adults.

Lewis is the senior author of the study, which appears today in Nature Aging. Sydney Bailes, a postdoc in the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former visiting student at MIT who earned her PhD from Boston University in 2026, are the lead authors of the paper.

During the deepest stages of sleep, also called non-REM sleep, high-amplitude, low-frequency waves contribute to physical recovery, memory consolidation, and many other functions. In a 2019 study, Lewis found that these slow waves are also critical for generating waves of CSF that help flush waste from the brain.

That finding led her to wonder whether reductions in slow waves in older people might also reduce CSF flow. Previous studies of aging have yielded conflicting evidence; some found that CSF flow goes down in older adults, while others found it goes up, but these studies did not monitor flow during sleep.
In the latest study, the researchers recruited volunteers in two age groups: 18 to 39 and 60 to 84. The tests lasted for about two hours and began late at night, so that participants would be sleepy.

The researchers used traditional fMRI to measure participants’ blood flow in the brain, along with a modified MRI technique, developed by Lewis, that measures CSF flow. While the subjects were in the scanner, the researchers also measured their brain waves using EEG.
articles.lede: MIT researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help remove debris from the brain during sleep, are significantly reduced in older adults.

‘Fossil record’ in stored blood samples lets scientists trace leukaemia back decades before diagnosis
articles.description: Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) develops over the decades before diagnosis, showing that in two-thirds of cases the first cancer-driving mutation had been acquired before the age of 20 – more than 50 years before diagnosis.
paragraphs: Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew
The discovery could help predict whether an individual will develop the disease years – or even decades – before symptoms arise, raising the possibility of preventing the disease before it develops.

In research published today in Nature, a team at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL) used blood samples collected annually, some dating back 15 years before diagnosis, as a ‘fossil record’ of the disease's development, tracing it step by step. Using ultra-sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical modelling, they estimated when each mutation arose and how quickly the affected cells multiplied and competed with other blood cells in the years prior to AML diagnosis.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer affecting around 2,700 people in the UK each year. Only around one in six survive five years after diagnosis. Many healthy older people carry blood cells with mutations also found in leukaemia, a condition known as clonal haematopoiesis, but only a small proportion develop AML. What has not been clear is why, because the process has never been tracked year by year in the run-up to diagnosis.

The researchers used samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS), in which around 50,000 women gave a blood sample every year for up to 11 years. The team studied 47 women who later developed AML, at an average age of 72, alongside matched samples from 46 women who stayed blood cancer-free.

This first mutation, acquired before age 20 in two-thirds of the women who developed AML, was followed by decades of slow growth – cells carrying it took years to double in number. Each additional mutation increased their growth rate around two- to three-fold, with cells carrying four cancer-driving mutations doubling in a matter of weeks.

The growth of these groups of cells, known as clones, proved remarkably predictable. Once a clone carrying a cancer-driving mutation was established, it expanded at a steady rate, slowing only when it ran out of room or was overtaken by a faster-growing clone. In practice, this means a clone's growth rate, measured from a few blood samples today, can be used to estimate how large that clone may become years and even decades into the future.

In at least a third of the AML cases, a clone had come to dominate the blood years before diagnosis, a phenomenon known as a ‘somatic sweep’. No such sweeps were seen in the women who remained blood cancer-free. The team confirmed the link with AML risk using UK Biobank data, finding that people with these sweeps were at greatly increased risk of developing the disease. The findings highlight the importance of recognising this potential warning sign, which standard genetic analysis often overlooks by mistaking these mutations for inherited variants.

Over 9 million lives could be saved every year if countries met WHO air quality guidelines
articles.description: Meeting the World Health Organization’s recommended annual guidelines for air pollution resulting from fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide has the potential to save more than 9 million lives a year in low- and middle-income countries, say University of Cambridge researchers.
paragraphs: Meeting the WHO’s air quality guideline values will not be straightforward, but low- and middle-income countries have a critical opportunity to shape healthier futures as their populations grow and their cities expand
It would also bring substantial savings from reduced illness, including lower healthcare costs and increased productivity as individuals take less time off work resulting from preventable illness.

Outdoor air pollution is the largest environmental threat to human health worldwide. It has been linked to increases in heart and lung diseases, including coronary heart disease, stroke, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and dementia. As well as the burden on individuals and their families, these diseases also have a substantial economic toll in terms of healthcare costs and lost productivity.

Because of the growing body of evidence of the impact of poor air quality, in 2021 the World Health Organization (WHO) revised its air quality guideline values for recommended maximum levels for several pollutants, including fine particulate matter (PM 2.5) and nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ).

PM 2.5 is particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 microns or less, tiny particles small enough that they can be inhaled deep into the lungs. These particles come from several sources, including vehicle emissions, power plants, industrial processes, wood burning stoves and fireplaces, and construction dust. They also form in the atmosphere because of complex chemical reactions involving other pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.

Nitrogen dioxide is one of the key pollutants that arise from burning fossil fuels. It is found in vehicle exhaust emissions, especially from diesel vehicles, and industrial emissions, as well as those from gas stoves and heaters.

The problem disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where air quality has generally deteriorated in line with large-scale urbanisation, economic development, and increasing use of cars and motor vehicles.

In a paper published today in Environment International, researchers at IMS Epidemiology, University of Cambridge, explored the potential health and economic benefits of improving air quality in 136 LMICs, focusing on PM 2.5 and NO 2.

The team combined detailed data from air pollution, population size and health with published evidence on the links between pollution, mortality and disease. They used computer modelling to estimate how deaths and new cases of illnesses might change if levels of particular pollutants fell to the WHO’s recommended air quality guidelines values and the more relaxed WHO interim targets. They also estimated the economic value of reducing the risk of premature death, alongside potential savings in healthcare and productivity costs.

‘Unique opportunity’ in study of colorectal cancer
articles.description: Dental medicine researchers will use statewide biobank to study link between microorganisms in mouth and disease.
paragraphs: Growing scientific evidence points to a potential role for specific oral microorganisms in the development and progression of colorectal cancer, yet relatively few studies have been able to examine oral, stool, and tumor samples collected from the same patients.

Now, researchers at Harvard School of Dental Medicine (HSDM) will have an opportunity to investigate how microorganisms originating in the mouth may interact with the gut and contribute to disease through a statewide biobank initiative supported by the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center.
The center is funding 13 projects at 11 academic medical centers and research institutions, to expand access to patient biospecimens and associated clinical data.

HSDM is among institutions participating in the colorectal cancer effort, providing researchers in the Feres Lab with access to a resource that could help answer questions that have been difficult to study using conventional datasets.

“This gives us a unique opportunity to advance our understanding of the oral-gut microbiome axis in colorectal cancer,” said Magda Feres, professor and chair of Oral Medicine, Infection & Immunity, who leads the Feres Lab at HSDM. “By integrating oral, stool, and tumor samples from the same patients with state-of-the-art multi-omics analyses and machine learning, we can move closer to breakthroughs in early diagnosis and prevention. We are thrilled to be part of this initiative.”

“By integrating oral, stool, and tumor samples from the same patients with state-of-the-art multi-omics analyses and machine learning, we can move closer to breakthroughs in early diagnosis and prevention.”

The project builds on a growing area of research examining connections between the oral microbiome — the community of microorganisms that inhabit the mouth — and diseases elsewhere in the body. Certain oral bacteria have been detected in colorectal tumors, raising questions about whether changes in the oral microbiome or the migration of specific microorganisms from the mouth to the gastrointestinal tract could contribute to the development or progression of CRC.

Determining the significance of those associations, however, requires researchers to look across different biological environments within the same individual. By analyzing matched oral, stool, and tumor specimens, the HSDM team will be able to investigate microbial and molecular patterns across the mouth, gut, and tumor rather than studying each site in isolation.

The researchers plan to apply multi-omics approaches to characterize the biological information contained in the samples and use machine learning to identify combinations of microbial and molecular features associated with colorectal cancer. Ultimately, those analyses could help researchers identify biomarkers that distinguish patients with colorectal cancer or potentially signal disease at an earlier stage.

“The rich data that can be collected here, combined with state-of-the-art methods to study the oral-gut microbiome and novel machine-learning predictive models, represent one of the best opportunities to date to identify microbial signatures associated with colorectal cancer and potentially inform future prevention strategies,”Feres said.

Leading AI models are biased against certain accents when scoring interviews, presentations and tests
cats: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
articles.description: UW researchers investigated how state-of-the-art language models, including two from Google and one from OpenAI, evaluated human speech in job interviews, confe
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence models replicate, and sometimes amplify, all sorts of human biases. In the last few years, University of Washington researchers have found AI has erased female characters from kids’ stories, favored job applicants of certain races and genders, and swayed human decisions.

Much bias research has focused on text and visuals. Yet people speak to AI models with increasing regularity, and AI tools are now used to screen job applicants and score oral presentations. Now, a UW-led team of researchers found that state-of-the-art AI models were biased against speakers with certain accents.

The team investigated how state-of-the-art multimodal language models, including two from Google and one from OpenAI, evaluated human speech in job interviews, conference presentations and spoken English proficiency tests. The models scored responses from voices speaking English with five different accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian. The AI models generally ranked Chinese and Nigerian accents the lowest, Indian in the middle, and American and British the highest. Even when the content was exactly the same and the models could accurately transcribe the speech, the systems ranked both the delivery and content higher for the American and British speakers.
The team presented its research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest, Hungary.

“People are now trusting audio AI models as sort of third-party evaluators, for hiring, for oral exams in education, for certain English tests in immigration — contexts where fairness really matters,” said co-lead author Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering. “So I was curious how models perceive speech from people who don’t speak with so-called ‘standard’ American accents.”

The team chose accents from five regions that have large populations of English speakers and where the researchers also had connections. Researchers then tested the accents in three different domains — hiring, presentations and English tests. To study differences at scale, they had AI voices from ElevenLabs read the same pieces of text to the AI models being tested. They validated the results with 52 human speakers from the five countries.
After some testing, the team focused the study on three proprietary AI models — Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash, and OpenAI’s GPT-Audio 1.5 — and one open-source model, Qwen 3 Omni.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models,” said senior author Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School, “because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting.”

The team had the AI voices read various scripts — interview responses, a class presentation, a conference presentation and English proficiency test responses — with the five different accents in both male and female voices. The four AI models then rated the responses on a scale of one to seven for both delivery and content, and gave a brief explanation for their scores.
articles.lede: Artificial intelligence models replicate, and sometimes amplify, all sorts of human biases.
