The project is called PYTHIA, which stands for “predictive platform for physiological and therapeutic health intervention and adaptive management.”

According to the project plan, the patch, which will capture clinical-grade health information in real time, will be powered by heat from the patient’s body. It could provide essential information to help clinicians diagnose heart failure and sepsis early, before the diseases have caused irreversible damage.

The researchers believe the minimally invasive device could also track the progress of a patient’s recovery after they are discharged from the hospital, and assist clinicians in developing more effective therapeutic approaches.

Heart disease is the number one cause of death in the U.S., while sepsis kills at least 350,000 U.S. adults each year and is the leading cause of death in hospitals, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

“We targeted these diseases because they are very lethal, but we also see opportunities for detecting biomarkers related to heart disease and sepsis to offer a solution that could really help improve diagnosis and treatment,” says principal investigator Ahmad Bahai, a professor of the practice in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics at MIT.

Bahai will be joined on the project by MIT researchers Joel Voldman, the William R. Brody Professor of EECS; Tim Swager, the John D. MacArthur Professor of Chemistry; Hadley Sikes, the Willard Henry Dow Professor in Chemical Engineering; and Collin Stultz, the Nina T. and Robert H. Rubin Professor of EECS; with additional clinical and industry collaborators.

“We have created an ecosystem of R&D, with MIT at the center of it, to facilitate not only leading-edge research, but also a path toward translation into a device that can be used in the clinic,” Bahai says. “Our goal with this project is to impact the future of personalized health care.”

PYTHIA grew out of the MIT Program for Health Sciences and Semiconductors (HS+S), which Bahai co-founded when he joined MIT three years ago. The program focuses on leveraging advances in semiconductor technology and nanotechnology to invent new, transformative approaches to diagnostics, therapeutics, and drug discovery.

Inspired by his previous successful work on continuous glucose monitors, Bahai conducts research on a wide range of technologies including electrochemical devices, optics, magnetics, and ultrasonics in his “Waves, Bites, and Molecules” lab. His group’s goal is to offer clinical-grade wearable devices that track biomarkers continuously to enable real-time intervention techniques.

About half of drinkers on GLP-1s say they imbibed less
articles.description: Study was sparked by reports of unexpected side effect amid skyrocketing popularity of drug for diabetes and weight loss.
paragraphs: Nearly half of drinkers who take GLP-1 medications have reported declines in consumption, with the effect higher among those at risk of unhealthy alcohol use, a new Harvard study shows.
The work, published in the journal JAMA Psychiatry in October, explores an unexpected and head-turning side effect of GLP-1s used to treat diabetes and obesity.

The drugs’ effectiveness, particularly for weight loss, have caused them to skyrocket in popularity and, as use spread, anecdotal evidence emerged about improvements in heart health and mental well-being, and reduced cravings for alcohol among patients.
Researchers from Harvard Medical School and McLean Hospital worked on the survey with collaborators from Brown, Duke, and Brandeis universities and Boston-based RAND Corporation.

The study grew out of work by senior author Haiden Huskamp, HMS’ Henry J. Kaiser Professor of Health Care Policy, and co-author Alisa Busch, HMS professor of psychiatry at McLean Hospital and associate professor of health care policy at HMS, on the underuse of medications to treat alcohol use disorder.
Anti-abuse medications have existed for decades — disulfiram, the oldest, has been around since the 1940s. But their use was vanishingly small.

Just 3 percent to 5 percent of those with a past alcohol abuse disorder reported using the drugs in a recent national survey, and only 10 percent of those seeking treatment have received the approved drugs.

“The national surveys show that far and away most people with alcohol-use disorder receive no treatment, period,” Busch said. “We have this evidence-based treatment that’s efficacious, so what are the patient characteristics, the clinician characteristics associated with being prescribed or not prescribed these medications?”

Busch, Huskamp, and their team took notice as accounts emerged about reduced cravings to drink among patients on GLP-1s. As reports multiplied and their effect on individuals became clearer, the two wanted to better understand the phenomenon on a population level.
“We wanted to really understand patient perception of this issue, and a large share of people taking GLP-1s are saying they’re drinking less,” Huskamp said.
articles.lede: Study was sparked by reports of unexpected side effect amid skyrocketing popularity of drug for diabetes and weight loss.

articles.title: MIT engineers design a safer, more efficient vaccination system for farmed fish
articles.description: MIT researchers developed water-resistant, food-grade microneedles that could be used to vaccinate farmed fish. The technology could help prevent disease outbreaks that cause substantial losses in aquaculture.
paragraphs: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."
Fish that are cultivated in pools or ponds are an increasingly important source of food around the world. Unfortunately, disease outbreaks can cause substantial losses in aquaculture.

Fish farmers use vaccines to prevent disease outbreaks just like regular farmers, but vaccinating a fish is a lot harder than vaccinating a cow. The most effective way to vaccinate fish today uses needles, but there are several downsides to this process, both for the fish and the farmers.

Now a team of researchers at MIT and the U.S. Department of Agriculture has developed a potentially better way to deliver vaccines. The approach uses water-resistant, food-grade microneedles that can lightly penetrate and remain attached to fish skin before decomposing. In a new paper published in ACS Nano, the researchers described their system and showed it could be used to deliver a range of cargos, such as bacterial vaccines.

“To feed the world we need more fish, which are a major source of protein and nutrition,” says Benedetto Marelli, a professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Aquaculture is a very effective way of producing a large amount of fish. Our approach could give farmers a more precise tool to maintain fish health. Farmers are really concerned about the health care of these fish, so providing them with better tools is really important.”

Joining Marelli on the paper are Meng Li, an MIT postdoc and first author on the paper; Jad Raad MEng ’24; Yunteng Cao PhD ’22, a postdoc at Yale University; Yue Hu, a former MIT postdoc; Colleen Wolfe MEng ’23; Doyoon Kim, a former MIT postdoc; Bradley Frank, a current MIT postdoc; and Gregory Wiens, a researcher at the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Center for Cool and Cold Water Aquaculture.

Aquaculture holds enormous potential to address food insecurity, reduce energy consumption, and decarbonize global food systems. In 2021, for the first time, farmed aquatic animals exceeded wild-caught aquatic animals in global food production by weight.

“The world’s population is going to grow by almost 2 billion people by 2050,” Marelli says. “Fish provide access to essential nutrition. They are high in protein and healthy fat, which are difficult to make, so the world is trying to produce more fish. But there are many challenges associated with fisheries.”

To prevent losses to disease, farmers use a range of automated and manual vaccination strategies, each with their own drawbacks. Some treatments can go into fish food, but those might not reach every fish. Another method is putting the treatment directly in a pool and immersing the fish in the treated water. That approach requires far higher quantities of treatment and, again, isn’t 100 percent effective.
articles.lede: MIT researchers developed water-resistant, food-grade microneedles that could be used to vaccinate farmed fish. The technology could help prevent disease outbreaks that cause substantial losses in aquaculture.

articles.title: MIT engineers create nanoparticles for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
articles.description: A nanoscale particle developed at MIT holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines. The particle could be adapted to carry many different antigens, to potentially treat individual patients’ tumors.
paragraphs: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."
A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines.

The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.
This type of delivery particle could be adapted to carry many different antigens, allowing for the creation of personalized vaccines to treat individual patients’ tumors, the researchers say.

“The great thing about this is that it’s modular and we could switch out different antigens on demand, so you could design it to be patient-specific and target a known antigen for a particular kind of cancer,” says Angela Belcher, the James Mason Crafts Professor of Biological Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering and a member of the Koch Institute.

Belcher is the senior author of the study, which appears today in the journal Advanced Healthcare Materials. Shengnan Huang, research scientist at the Koch Institute, is the paper’s lead author. Jack Rudrum, Huaiyao Peng, and Hao Nghi Luu, graduate students at the Koch Institute, are also authors of the paper.

For more than 20 years, Belcher’s lab has been deploying the M13 bacteriophage in a variety of applications. This virus, which is harmless to humans, consists of a single strand of DNA coated in a protein shell, or capsid.

Belcher has previously developed techniques for generating materials by engineering these viruses to self-assemble into nanoscale scaffolds. By coating these scaffolds with inorganic materials, they can create functional devices such as batteries, semiconductors, solar cells, and catalysts, with precise control over the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of the materials.
More recently, Belcher’s lab has been developing methods to control features of the phage that could allow it to be repurposed for medical applications, including vaccine delivery.

“We’re taking this toolkit that we’ve worked on and developed over decades and formatting it to be specific for vaccine therapeutics,” Belcher says. “Some of the lessons learned from making batteries and all these other things are now being fine-tuned to make personalized vaccines.”

articles.description: MIT researchers showed they can track muscle movement using tiny magnetic beads implanted in the muscle. These measurements could make it easier for people with certain types of amputations to control their prosthetic limbs.

You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."

MIT researchers have shown that they can accurately track muscle movement using tiny magnetic beads implanted in the muscle. These measurements could make it easier for people with certain types of amputations to control their prosthetic limbs.

For decades, researchers have been working to develop neuroprosthetic limbs, which use neural information from muscles remaining after an amputation to guide the prosthetic limb. Measurements of a muscle’s length, velocity and activation can be fed into the control algorithms that guide the limbs, allowing individuals with leg amputation to walk with a more natural gait, or those with arm amputation to manipulate objects more effectively.

Until now, these devices have relied on muscle activity measurements from electrodes placed on the surface of the skin. However, those measurements have not proven reliable enough to ensure safety while walking with a neuroprosthetic leg.
The MIT team hopes that their new magnetic tracking system, which offers more accurate measurements, will enable commercial development of such limbs.

“For four decades, the standard methodology for neurally controlling prostheses has been to use skin electrodes to measure muscle activation. However, to control a prosthetic limb, joint position, torque, or impedance has to be controlled, and one cannot directly determine such mechanical signals using electrical activation alone,” says Hugh Herr, a professor of media arts and sciences, co-director of the K. Lisa Yang Center for Bionics at MIT, an associate member of MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, and the senior author of the new study.
In the new study, which appears today in Nature Sensors, the researchers demonstrated the accuracy of the magnetic measurements in three participants with below-knee amputations.

“This interface is minimally invasive, so it could be accessible to more people. You place two beads in the muscle and you have access to all of this rich information about the muscle dynamics,” says Christopher Shallal, an MIT graduate student in the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology and one of the lead authors of the paper.
The paper’s other lead author is Cameron Taylor PhD ’20, an assistant professor of biomedical engineering at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

For many years, Herr’s lab has been developing human-machine interfaces that can be used to control an artificial limb in a way that makes it more like using a natural limb. Obtaining accurate measurements of how the user is moving the muscles at the amputation site is critical to the success of this type of prosthesis.

articles.title: Capturing the complete process of embryonic development
articles.description: MIT researchers created a detailed lineage map of cell divisions and fates in a developing mouse embryo. This map of mammalian development could have broad implications for understanding birth defects and cancer.
paragraphs: For decades, scientists have been able to look at individual moments in the development of an embryo: a snapshot of a developing brain, a picture of how the heart takes shape, or a glimpse of cells beginning to form the nervous system.

A new study out of the lab of MIT Professor Jonathan Weissman, a member of the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator, offers one of the most detailed views yet of how a mammal is built, cell by cell.

By following the family history of over a million cells as a mouse embryo develops, the researchers have created a kind of developmental blueprint, or movie, showing how cells divide and ultimately become the tissues and organs in the body.

This open-access work, published Oct. 8 in the journal Cell, in collaboration with Zachary Smith’s group at Yale University and the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics, provides a comprehensive view of a process that has long been studied in pieces: how a single fertilized egg gives rise to hundreds of different kinds of cells, arranged in the right places and at the right times to build an animal.
“This is really a view of how the information in the genome plays out over space and time to go from linear DNA to a three-dimensional animal,” Weissman says.

The map could have broad implications for understanding birth defects and cancer. Many birth defects arise when cells change course as tissues and organs are being assembled. A detailed map of typical development could help researchers pinpoint where and when those processes go awry. In cancer, the same approach could help scientists trace when cells acquire traits such as the ability to spread or resist treatment.

The map could also inform stem cell research by revealing the sequence of cell states that leads to mature, functional cell types. In the 1980s, scientists ventured into similar territory by painstakingly following the development of Caenorhabditis elegans, a tiny worm whose transparent body contains only about 1,000 cells. Using microscopy, they could trace how individual cells divided and where their descendants ended up. But achieving something similar in a mammal was a challenge on a vastly different scale. Mammalian embryos contain far more cells, develop inside the uterus — out of sight — and do not follow a completely predetermined script. The new study tackles this challenge using a technology developed in the Weissman Lab called PEtracer. The system acts somewhat like a flight recorder inside a cell. PEtracer makes small, heritable changes to DNA that are passed down as cells divide. By reading those changes later, scientists can work backward to reconstruct which cells came from which ancestors, essentially building a family tree for the cells in the developing embryo.

In this work, the researchers combined these family trees with information about what genes were turned on in each cell and where these cells were located in the embryo. They analyzed over a million cells from mouse embryos collected at multiple points during development, allowing them to follow not just where cells ended up, but when they began heading toward particular fates.
articles.lede: MIT researchers created a detailed lineage map of cell divisions and fates in a developing mouse embryo. This map of mammalian development could have broad implications for understanding birth defects and cancer.

articles.title: How the biggest Alzheimer’s risk gene disrupts the process of insulating neurons
articles.description: MIT researchers discovered how the biggest Alzheimer’s risk gene disrupts the process of insulating neurons: The APOE4 gene variant suppresses molecular signaling needed for oligodendrocytes to myelinate neurons. The researchers also demonstrated a proof-of-concept fix.
paragraphs: One of the main ways that the APOE4 gene variant, the biggest genetic risk factor for late onset Alzheimer’s disease, undermines brain circuit function is by disrupting the process of insulating neurons with a fatty sheath that optimizes their electrical transmission. A new study led by neuroscientists at the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory at MIT provides several lines of evidence to implicate a specific molecular pathway in that disruption, and uses that insight to demonstrate an intervention for preventing it in lab experiments.

The study, published Oct. 15 in Cell Stem Cell, shows that APOE4 leads to a suppression of “Wnt” signaling in the oligodendrocyte cells that provide neurons with a fatty insulation, called myelin. When Wnt signaling is deficient, they showed, the cells accumulate droplets of lipids rather than deploying fats to properly myelinate the neurons’ axon branches. When the researchers restored Wnt signaling in APOE4-carrying oligodendrocytes, myelination rebounded, both in human cell cultures and in mice modeling Alzheimer’s.

The research team, led by Picower Professor Li-Huei Tsai and study lead author Leyla Akay PhD ’25, a former graduate student in Tsai’s lab, discovered Wnt’s key role via multiple methods, including a screen in which they used CRISPR gene editing to systematically knock out each protein-coding gene in the genome, one by one, in cultures of human APOE4-carrying oligodendrocytes. The screen showed that when genes promoting Wnt activity in oligodendrocytes were lacking, lipid droplets accumulated, and that when genes suppressing Wnt were lacking, lipid droplets were, too.

“This proof of principle of doing CRISPR screens for genetic modifiers of APOE4-associated lipid accumulation in a central nervous system cell type is very exciting,” says Tsai, who also directs MIT’s Aging Brain Initiative. “I think this type of screen not only provides new insights into cellular pathways contributing to lipid metabolism defects, but really also has the potential to provide new targets for drug development.”

In 2022, Tsai’s Lab, led by Akay, Djuna Von Maydell PhD ’25, Jose Davila-Velderrain, and Joel Blanchard (also a co-author of the new study), showed that APOE4 caused lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes and upset myelination. But, Akay says, that droplet accumulation could happen for many reasons. The new study sought to dig deeper into the underlying molecular mechanisms.

“This CRISPR screen allowed us an unbiased way to test every single possibility,” Akay says. “What kind of lipid enzymes are involved in this process? And what are upstream pathways that could be targeted?”

In parallel with the CRISPR screen, the team also analyzed the chromatin accessibility of the DNA in human oligodendrocyte cell cultures and in postmortem human brain samples, in each case comparing APOE4-carrying samples to ones carrying the neutral APOE3 variant. This analysis of ATAC-seq data allowed them to assess which genes were most accessible for expression versus which ones were locked down from transcription. The chromatin analysis showed that genes promoting Wnt signaling were less accessible in APOE4 carriers.
articles.lede: MIT researchers discovered how the biggest Alzheimer’s risk gene disrupts the process of insulating neurons: The APOE4 gene variant suppresses molecular signaling needed for oligodendrocytes to myelinate neurons.

articles.title: A soft robot could help doctors diagnose and treat disorders of the small intestine
articles.description: MIT engineers designed a robotic enteroscope that can move easily through the narrow passage of the small intestine, allowing it to perform imaging, deliver drugs, and remove small polyps or tissue samples for biopsy.
paragraphs: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."

Disorders of the small intestine are often difficult to diagnose and treat. More than 20 feet long, an inch in diameter, and located deep within the body, this organ is harder to access than other parts of the digestive tract, such as the colon or stomach.

To overcome those challenges, MIT engineers have designed a new robotic enteroscope that can move easily through the narrow passage of the small intestine, allowing it to perform imaging, deliver drugs, and remove small polyps or tissue samples for biopsy.

In designing the new robot, the researchers were inspired by the locomotion of snakes, as well as the scaly skin that helps them gain traction on slippery surfaces. A special textured coating helps the robot remain attached to the mucosal lining of the intestine as it inches its way through the narrow tube.
Similar to an endoscope, the robot contains a variety of tools to help detect and treat any abnormalities that it might encounter.

“When we evaluate the small intestine, we do it for either diagnosis or treatment. If we find a little polyp that needs to be removed, this robot allows us to take a biopsy or remove it,” says Giovanni Traverso, professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, a gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and an associate member of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.

Traverso is the senior author of the study, which appears today in Science Robotics. The paper’s lead authors are former MIT postdoc Binbin Ying, who is now an assistant professor at University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; MIT graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran; and former MIT research scientist Sahab Babaee.
The most common problems that doctors need to evaluate within the small intestine include bleeding, lesions, and blockages.

Currently, the only way to diagnose those intestinal complications is with a procedure known as double balloon enteroscopy. During the procedure, an enteroscope advances through the small intestine as a health care worker alternately inflates and deflates two balloons that help propel it through the tract.
This process is slow and laborious, so the MIT team wanted to design an alternative enteroscope that would be easier to control and could move faster through the intestine.
articles.lede: MIT engineers designed a robotic enteroscope that can move easily through the narrow passage of the small intestine, allowing it to perform imaging, deliver drugs, and remove small polyps or tissue samples for biopsy.

Implantable device uses ultrasound to improve drug delivery to the brain
articles.description: MIT researchers designed an implantable drug-delivery device to help prevent recurrence of glioblastoma. Ultrasound transducers printed onto the device use sound waves to help drugs pass through the blood-brain barrier.

Patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain tumor, usually undergo surgery to remove the tumor. However, it’s difficult for surgeons to remove all of the cancer cells, and the tumor often recurs.

MIT researchers have now designed an implantable drug-delivery device that they hope could help prevent recurrence of glioblastoma. Their device contains a reservoir that can release drugs over an extended period, along with ultrasound transducers that use sound waves to help drugs spread farther through the brain and bypass the blood-brain barrier.

Such a device could be implanted in the brain during surgery, then gradually release drugs that would help kill the remaining tumor cells. After implantation, a wireless controller can be used to program the exact ultrasound dosages to be delivered, enhancing the reach of the delivered therapy.

“We have 24 transducers in one ultrasound array, which can help a given drug bypass the blood-brain barrier and enhance the drug infusion. The device also gives doctors options in terms of the size, the length, and the number of infusions,” says Canan Dagdeviren, an associate professor of media arts and sciences at MIT and the senior author of the study.
In a paper appearing today in the journal Device, the researchers showed that their ultrasound device allowed molecules to spread further after being released, in tissue models and in a mouse study.
MIT graduate student Sarah Ornellas and Jason Hou PhD ’26 are the lead authors of the study.

Glioblastoma is a rare but deadly cancer, with a little more than 10,000 cases diagnosed in the United States per year. On average, patients survive 12 to 15 months after diagnosis. Patients typically undergo surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible, followed by radiation and chemotherapy.

Chemotherapy drugs are usually given either as pills or an intravenous infusion, but in recent years, scientists have developed drug-delivery wafers and hydrogels that can be implanted directly in the skull. That can help to eliminate the side effects of chemotherapy and ensure that a higher concentration of the drug reaches the brain.

Those devices work by passive diffusion of drugs, but the MIT team wanted to design a new device that would allow for greater control of the timing of drug release. They also wanted to incorporate ultrasound arrays to enhance the distribution of drug molecules.

articles.title: White paper sets out blueprint for keeping innovation in the UK
articles.description: The loss of jobs, laboratories and research capability that follows when promising technology and life sciences companies migrate from Britain should be addressed through contractual commitments from investors or acquirers to maintain a defined UK presence for a fixed period, says a new white paper.
paragraphs: “Too many businesses are born in Britain but build their futures elsewhere. We should welcome global capital and negotiate harder to keep research, skills and high-value jobs at home. This timely whitepaper offers a practical way to do both.”

In Should I stay or should I go? A Pragmatic Path to Keeping UK Innovation at Home, Pascal Levensohn (founder of Levensohn Venture Partners LLC, Executive Chairman of Dolby Family Ventures, Chair of the Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board and Fellow of Cambridge Judge Business School) says such a commitment can be implemented without difficult and time-consuming legislation.

He argues that the debate over world-beating firms leaving the UK has conflated two separate questions – the health of the UK’s capital markets and the robustness of its innovation ecosystem – and has therefore misdiagnosed the problem. The commercial, rather than legislative, solution he proposes is a practical approach that can keep investment and high-quality jobs in the UK while the larger capital-markets debate proceeds.

“Foreign acquisition is not the problem – and neither is foreign ownership,” says Levensohn. “A central problem is the failure to distinguish between three different forms of migration – of ownership and financial returns, of domicile and listing venue, and of productive capability.

“Treated as a single, inevitable sequence, they obscure the opportunities for targeted intervention and invite the assumption that the first or second must lead to the third. It is the third that constitutes the avoidable national loss: a listing or an acquisition followed by the migration or erosion of substantive UK productive capability.”

The solution he proposes in the paper is that: “The UK – government, universities, founders and the investment community together – should far more forcefully seek commitments from international investors and acquirers to create jobs and maintain a meaningful UK footprint for companies born in the UK, nourished by UK taxpayer investment, and first taking root in UK soil. The fruits from the UK’s innovation orchard can be harvested – ownership can change, returns can flow abroad – without pulling up the tree.”

The paper quantifies what is at stake. Between 2015 and 2025, on average 40 UK deep-tech companies were acquired each year. If just 20 of them negotiated a binding commitment resulting in 25 net new UK-based jobs, sustained for the five-year life of the commitment, the programme would generate £312.5 million of additional gross value added a year by the fifth year and would cumulate to £2.5 billion over ten years.

Levensohn cites precedents showing the feasibility of the approach, including the undertakings Japan’s SoftBank gave when it acquired Cambridge-based chip designer Arm in 2016 – to at least double Arm’s UK headcount within five years and keep its global headquarters in Cambridge – which the Takeover Panel’s independent supervisor later verified were honoured. Arm’s subsequent 2023 Nasdaq listing illustrates that a change of listing venue is not, in itself, the loss of UK productive capability.

Q&A: The “collision” between AI, your brain, and society
articles.description: Heavy use of artificial intelligence can lead to a kind of cognitive atrophy, in which people fail to develop and retain essential thinking skills, MIT Professor Eric So contends in his book, “The Collision: What AI does to Us.”
paragraphs: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."

As artificial intelligence use becomes more widespread, scholars are working to understand its effects on the people who use it. MIT Professor Eric So offers one of the most complete syntheses yet, in his new book, “The Collision: What AI Does to Us,” published this month by W.W. Norton. Recognizing that AI offers opportunities to complete work faster, and in some cases has been turned into useful domain-specific tools, So nonetheless looks at the costs of relying on it too broadly. He contends that heavy use of AI can lead to a kind of cognitive atrophy, in which people fail to develop and retain essential thinking skills. In general, he says, evidence shows that our ability to learn gets dramatically better when we wrestle with material, work through initial failures, keep iterating, and in the process acquire better thinking skills while retaining more knowledge.

These conclusions are drawn from recent research by So and others, in academia and industry, including analysis from AI firms themselves, such as an Anthropic study showing that about half of queries from college students were low-effort queries for simple answers. So also weaves personal reflections into his narrative — having long studied financial markets and behavior, he is familiar with analyzing how new tools and information affect our decisions. MIT News talked to So, who is the Sloan Distinguished Professor of Global Economics and Behavioral Science in the MIT Sloan School of Management, about the book.

A: I wrote this book in response to patterns I was seeing in myself and other individuals. I open the book with this story where I was instinctively reaching for AI to help me think through problems I normally would have handled myself. A colleague had reached out for assistance and I had essentially taken her question and written half a sentence, then said, “ChatGPT, help me finish this professionally.” I made a few light edits and sent it off. And I sat back and really felt incredibly concerned about how I had removed my own thinking from the process.

I have found students are outsourcing their thinking to AI, rather than thinking through things themselves, turning to it to answer homework that would normally help them build mastery in a subject. We need to start understanding what this technology is doing to us and how it interacts with human cognition and our psychology, and give people some practical insights.
Q: Part of that means understanding the incentives people have to use AI, or how the allure of AI takes hold, even when there are long-term costs, in your view.

A: There are converging factors drawing us to AI. For example we have a real biological instinct to conserve our mental energy, and socially, we face situations where AI is used by other people to race ahead, and it rachets up the pressure on everyone else to use AI. Combine that with the problems detecting AI use in a practical way, and all these factors create what I call “AI gravity,” this constant pull to use AI. It’s not simply a matter of telling people to think for themselves. At this moment we’re in, AI is colliding with society.
articles.lede: Heavy use of artificial intelligence can lead to a kind of cognitive atrophy, in which people fail to develop and retain essential thinking skills, MIT Professor Eric So contends in his book, “The Collision: What AI does to Us.”

articles.title: Reprogrammed NK immune cells target cancer and autoimmune disorders
articles.description: MIT engineers developed lipid nanoparticles that deliver mRNA to program natural killer (NK) cells inside the body. These CAR NK cells could be used to treat T cell cancers or autoimmune disorders caused by autoreactive T cells.
paragraphs: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."

MIT engineers have developed a new way to program natural killer (NK) immune cells to target cancerous T cells or T cells that have become autoreactive, leading to diseases such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Using their new technique, the researchers can reprogram NK cells to target diseased T cells without ever removing the NK cells from the patient’s body. Instead, they use lipid nanoparticles to deliver messenger RNA directly to NK cells. These mRNA molecules encode proteins that allow the NK cells to seek and destroy the dysfunctional T cells.

Known as CAR NK cells, these cells could be deployed against a variety of diseases. The MIT team’s new approach could bypass one of the major obstacles to using these cells, which is the time and expense of manufacturing them outside the body.

“The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells,” says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT’s Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT’s Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the study, which appears today in Nature Biotechnology. The paper’s lead authors are MIT postdoc Yuang Chen and MIT graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, the David H. Koch Institute Professor at MIT, is also an author.

Over the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven new cancer treatments based on engineered T cells called chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. Chimeric antigen receptors are proteins that can be embedded into T cells, allowing them to detect a target antigen, such as a cancer protein. When the target is detected, the T cell becomes activated and destroys the target cell.
This approach has had great success in treating blood cancers, primarily those that originate from B cells, including several types of leukemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma.

To make CAR T cells, doctors take a blood sample from the patient. The sample is sent to a lab where the T cells are isolated and then engineered to express the CAR protein. When enough CAR T cells have been generated, they are shipped back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

In recent years, scientists have begun using a similar strategy to create CAR NK cells. One potential advantage of CAR NK cells over CAR T cells is that they could be used to kill diseased T cells. Using CAR T cells to treat T cell diseases often doesn’t work well because T cells that are engineered to target T cell proteins may end up killing each other, in addition to the diseased T cells. That issue doesn’t arise when using NK cells to target T cells.
articles.lede: MIT engineers developed lipid nanoparticles that deliver mRNA to program natural killer (NK) cells inside the body. These CAR NK cells could be used to treat T cell cancers or autoimmune disorders caused by autoreactive T cells.

Social brain research offers new insights into how strangers become friends
articles.description: The closer two people grow, the more alike their brains work – or so the assumption goes. Two ETH Zurich studies challenge this idea by examining the brain activity of younger and older adults who drew together over several weeks. Despite growing closer, the similarity of their brain activity did not simply increase.
paragraphs: With the help of portable brain sensors, ETH Zurich researchers tracked, week by week, how the brain activity of two people changed as they got to know one another. This is the first study in this research field to include older adults aged between 70 and 85 years.

When younger and older adults draw shared pictures together over several weeks, they get to know each other better. Their brain activity, however, does not necessarily become more similar as a result.
The results suggest that the extent to which two people’s brain activity becomes more similar depends on how fluently they can predict and anticipate each other’s behaviour.

What happens in the brain when two people engage in joint creative activity and build a new relationship with one another in the process? ETH cognitive scientist, Ryssa Moffat investigated this question. She is a postdoctoral researcher at the Social Brain Sciences Lab within the Chair of Cognitive and Social Neuroscience.

Her study has now been published in the journal PLOS Biology. The setting was as follows: over a period of six weeks, 61 pairs met six times to engage in drawing together. The participants came from a younger age group (18 to 35 years) and an older age group (70 to 85 years) and were divided into 31 cross-generational pairs and 30 pairs of the same age.

At the outset, the participants did not know each other and first had to become familiar with one another. At each session, the pairs first drew individually on separate sheets of paper, then drew together twice on a single sheet of paper. They were free to decide whether to take turns or draw simultaneously. They were allowed to converse throughout the session but were instructed to remain silent while drawing.

At each session, the researchers recorded participants’ brain activity with the help of wearable brain sensors. This enabled the researchers to investigate how the process of getting to know one another was reflected in the pairs’ brain activity. At the same time, the mobile sensors ensured that participants could move and respond to each other naturally, as in everyday life, without distorting the recorded signals.

The similarity of the brain activity was particularly crucial for the ETH researchers: to what extent do the brains of two people synchronise during an encounter? And how does this synchronisation change over the course of repeated sessions? The focus was not on whether a pattern of brain activity corresponds to a specific subjective feeling such as liking or irritation.

Moffat was interested in what researchers call ‘inter-brain synchrony’: when people perform a shared task such as drawing, each person's brain reacts continuously to the other person's actions – and the brains can be said to be 'synchronised' when similar changes in brain activity occur simultaneously in both people
articles.lede: The closer two people grow, the more alike their brains work – or so the assumption goes. Two ETH Zurich studies challenge this idea by examining the brain activity of younger and older adults who drew together over several weeks.
